sections.title: Pleomorphic Adenoma (Benign Mixed Cell Tumour)
content: Commonest lacrimal neoplasm: Accounts for up to 20% of all lacrimal fossa lesions.
Origin: Derived from epithelial and mesenchymal tissue.
Lobe Involvement: May arise from either lobe, most commonly the orbital lobe.
Demographics: Occurs in middle age; slight ♂ bias (♂:♀ 1.5:1).
Malignant Transformation: Occurs in <3% in 10y and 10–20% in 20y.
Clinical Features: Gradual painless proptosis (inferonasal), upper lid swelling, diplopia, palpable mass (orbital lobe tumours may not be palpable).
Globe Effects: Indentation may cause choroidal folds ± hypermetropic shift.

rows: Round, lobulated lesion, typically medium/high reflectivity.
Expansion of lacrimal fossa, indentation of globe, well-circumscribed and slightly nodular tumour, calcification in 3%.
Surgical removal of whole tumour with intact pseudocapsule by anterior (palpebral lobe) or lateral (orbital lobe) orbitotomy.
Excellent with complete excision; needs prolonged follow-up for malignant transformation even if clearance is complete.

sections.title: CRITICAL WARNING: Pleomorphic Adenoma
content: DO NOT PERFORM PRIOR BIOPSY: Risk of seeding.
Patient must be warned regarding subsequent KCS (Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca).

sections.title: Lacrimal Carcinomas
content: Commonest malignant lacrimal tumour: Adenoid cystic carcinoma.
Other types: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma and pleomorphic adenocarcinoma.
Clinical: Rapid proptosis, ophthalmoparesis, and orbital pain.
Spread: Sensory disturbance from perineural spread is common.
Imaging: Irregular poorly defined lesion; bony destruction and calcification (20–30%).
Treatment: Seldom curative; exenteration ± radiotherapy.
Prognosis: Very poor with high mortality.

branches: Slow-growing tumour of glial tissue (Children focus)
Presentation: Gradual dVA (often stabilizes), disc swelling/atrophy, proptosis
Imaging: Fusiform enlargement of optic nerve ± chiasmal mass
Management: Observation (good vision), MRI monitoring, Surgery (reduced vision/pain/chiasm threat), Chemo/Radio (chiasmal/midbrain involvement)

sections.title: Optic Nerve Sheath Meningioma
content: Rare benign tumour of meningothelial cells; middle age focus.
Gender: Slight ♀ bias (♀:♂ 1.5:1).
Association: Neurofibromatosis-2.
Presentation: Gradual dVA, disc swelling/atrophy, optic disc collateral vessels (30%), proptosis, ophthalmoparesis.
Imaging Hallmark: Tubular enlargement with ‘tram-track’ enhancement of the sheath ± calcification.
Management: Observation if VA is good. Surgery for blind eyes, severe proptosis, or chiasm threat.
Prognosis: Good for life.

rows: Childhood; NF-1; ‘bag-of-worms’ mass; S-shaped lid deformity; Poorly defined/unencapsulated; Hard to excise (debulking needed).
Adulthood; Gradual proptosis; Well circumscribed; Straightforward surgical excision.
Slow-growing/Benign (rarely malignant); NF association; Adulthood; Superior orbit; Cystic non-tender mass; Good prognosis with excision.

sections.title: Vascular Tumours: Cavernous Haemangioma
content: Commonest benign orbital neoplasm in adults.
Pathology: Hamartoma of dilated large vascular spaces lined by endothelial cells.
Presentation: Young adulthood; accelerated growth during pregnancy.
Location: 80% Intraconal.
Features: Axial proptosis, restricted motility, globe indentation (choroidal folds/hypermetropic shift), dVA.
Rare Sign: Gaze-evoked amaurosis (apical retrobulbar lesions).
US: Well-defined, round intraconal lesion with high internal reflectivity.
CT/MRI: Well-circumscribed intraconal lesion; mild/moderate enhancement; possible thrombosis.
Treatment: Observation (most); excision (symptomatic).

rows: Hamartoma; Kasabach–Merritt syndrome (dplatelets, dHb, dclotting factors) or cardiac failure in large tumours. Treatment: Corticosteroids (topical/intralesional/systemic), Propranolol, Surgery.
‘Strawberry naevus’ (dermis); appears <2mo, full size at 1y, involutes by 6y. Risk: Amblyopia/astigmatism.
Posterior to septum; proptosis worsens with Valsalva/crying; partial involution.

Rare hamartoma (childhood); size increases with Valsalva/head-down posture. Superficial: Transilluminable cystic lid/conjunctival spaces. Deep: 'Chocolate cyst' (haemorrhage). Treatment: Observation, sclerosing agents, Bleomycin, Onyx®, drainage, or surgery (difficult/friable).

sections.title: Lymphoproliferative Disorders
content: Spectrum: Benign hyperplasia to malignant lymphomas (85% B-lymphocytes). Classified by WHO system.
Benign Reactive Lymphoid Hyperplasia: Polyclonal; superolateral orbit/lacrimal gland; firm rubbery mass. 25% progress to lymphoma by 5y. Rx: Steroids, Radio, Rituximab.
Atypical Lymphoid Hyperplasia: Intermediate; homogeneous pattern with larger nuclei.
Malignant Orbital Lymphoma: Low-grade B-cell (Non-Hodgkin); commonest is Marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of MALT (40–70%).
Lymphoma Stats: 50% are primary tumours; 25% bilateral; up to 60% systemic involvement within 5y. Rx: Systemic work-up mandatory; Radio/Chemo/Antibody.

sections.title: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis
content: Rare proliferative disorder of childhood.
Spectrum: Eosinophilic granuloma (benign/unifocal) to Letterer–Siwe form (disseminated).
Presentation: Rapid proptosis with superotemporal swelling.
Bilateral involvement occurs in disseminated forms.
Treatment: Surgical excision is usually curative.

sections.title: Rhabdomyosarcoma: The Pediatric Emergency
content: Commonest primary orbital malignancy in children; 87% present <15y.
Types: Embryonal (commonest), Alveolar, Pleomorphic.
Clinical: Acute/subacute proptosis, ptosis, and inflammation (mimics orbital cellulitis).
Investigations: US (high internal flow on Doppler); CT/MRI (mass ± bony erosion).
Mandatory: Biopsy + Systemic work-up.
Rx: Surgery (localized) or Combined Radio/Chemo (extensive).

rows: Commonest adult mesenchymal tumour; superonasal location; benign or malignant.
Complete surgical excision; recurrences common; metastases rare.
Aggressive; rapid proptosis, restricted motility, CN involvement. Scirrhous (Breast/Gastric) may cause enophthalmos.
Half of cases precede primary tumour diagnosis.

sections.title: Vascular Lesions: Varices & AV Fistulae
content: Orbital Varices: Congenital; intermittent proptosis (worse with Valsalva/coughing); phleboliths on imaging. Rx: Surgery (difficult) or sclerosant/coil.

Carotid–Cavernous Fistula (Direct): High-flow; Trauma/Spontaneous; Pulsatile proptosis + audible bruit, chemosis, iIOP, ophthalmoparesis, RAPD, disc swelling. Rx: Catheter embolization (>85% success).
Dural Shunt (Indirect CCF): Low-flow; Spontaneous (Hypertension); Episcleral venous arterialization, chemosis. Rx: 40% spontaneously thrombose; intervention for glaucoma/pain/dVA.
AV Fistula Investigations: US/CT/MRI show dilated superior ophthalmic vein and thick EOMs.

sections.title: Prognosis Summary
content: Pleomorphic Adenoma: Excellent with complete excision.
Lacrimal Carcinoma: Very poor; high mortality.
Optic Nerve Glioma: Good for life (if restricted to nerve).
Schwannoma: Good with excision.
Langerhans (Eosinophilic): Curative with excision.
Dural Shunt: 40% Spontaneous resolution.

sections.content: An exhaustive clinical guide detailing the epidemiology, clinical features, investigations, and management of orbital neoplasms and vascular anomalies including lacrimal, neural, lymphoproliferative, and metastatic conditions.

sections.title: Lacrimal Gland: Pleomorphic Adenoma (Benign Mixed Cell Tumour)

branches: Epidemiology: Commonest lacrimal neoplasm (up to 20% of fossa lesions). Middle age, slight male bias (♂:♀ 1.5:1).
Origin: Derived from epithelial and mesenchymal tissue. Arises from either lobe, most commonly the orbital lobe.

Clinical Features: Gradual painless inferonasal proptosis, upper lid swelling, diplopia, palpable mass (orbital lobe tumours may not be palpable). Globe indentation: choroidal folds ± hypermetropic shift.

rows: Round, lobulated lesion, typically medium/high reflectivity.
Expansion of lacrimal fossa, globe indentation, well-circumscribed/nodular, calcification (3%).
Removal of whole tumour with intact pseudocapsule without prior biopsy (risk of seeding). Anterior (palpebral) or lateral (orbital) orbitotomy.
Excellent with complete excision. Warn regarding KCS. Prolonged follow-up needed for malignant transformation.

sections.title: Lacrimal Carcinomas: High Alert
content: Commonest malignant: Adenoid cystic carcinoma, followed by mucoepidermoid and pleomorphic adenocarcinoma.
Clinical: Rapid proptosis, ophthalmoparesis, orbital pain, or sensory disturbance from perineural spread.
Imaging: Irregular poorly defined lesion, bony destruction, calcification (20–30%).
Treatment: Seldom curative; exenteration ± radiotherapy.
Prognosis: Very poor with high mortality.

sections.title: Neural Tumours: Optic Nerve Glioma
content: Uncommon slow-growing glial tissue tumour; usually occurs in children.
Strong association with Neurofibromatosis-1 (NF-1).
Presentation: Gradual dVA (often stabilizes), disc swelling or atrophy, and proptosis.
Distribution: Isolated nerve (22%), Chiasm (72%), often involves midbrain/hypothalamus.
Imaging: Fusiform enlargement of optic nerve ± chiasmal mass.
Observation: For isolated nerve tumours distant from chiasm, good vision, non-disfiguring proptosis. Monitor with serial MRI.
Surgical Excision: For reduced vision, pain, severe proptosis, or posterior spread threatening chiasm.
Other Tx: Chemotherapy or radiotherapy for chiasmal/midbrain involvement.
Prognosis: Good for nerve-restricted; worsens with posterior involvement.

rows: Gradual dVA, disc swelling/atrophy, disc collateral vessels (30%), proptosis, ophthalmoparesis.
Adulthood. Superior orbit. Non-tender mass (often cystic), proptosis, dVA, restricted motility.
Observation if VA good. Excision for blind eyes, severe proptosis, or chiasm threat.

sections.title: Neurofibroma Variants
content: Plexiform Neurofibroma: Childhood onset, strongly associated with NF-1. 'Bag-of-worms' mass with S-shaped lid deformity. Poorly defined, not encapsulated. Surgery: difficult, may need repeated debulking.
Isolated Neurofibroma: Adulthood onset, gradual proptosis. Well-circumscribed. Surgery: usually straightforward.

branches: Type: Commonest benign orbital neoplasm in adults. Hamartoma of large vascular spaces.
Presentation: Young adulthood, accelerated in pregnancy. Usually intraconal (80%).
Clinical: Axial proptosis, restricted motility, globe indentation (choroidal folds/hypermetropic shift), dVA. Rare: amaurosis.
Investigations: US (well-defined, high internal reflectivity). CT/MRI (intraconal, mild/mod enhancement, possible thrombosis).
Treatment: Observation for asymptomatic; excision for symptomatic.

sections.title: Vascular: Capillary Haemangioma
content: Definition: Hamartoma. Massive tumours may cause Kasabach-Merritt syndrome (dplatelets, dhb, dclotting factors) or high-output cardiac failure.
Superficial ('Strawberry Naevus'): Confined to dermis. Bright red, appears <2mo, full size by 1y, involutes by 6y. May cause amblyopia/astigmatism.
Deep Lesions: Posterior to septum. Variable proptosis (worsens with Valsalva/crying). Partial involution with time.
Treatment: Topical/intralesional/systemic corticosteroids, Systemic propranolol, Surgical excision.

sections.title: Vascular: Lymphangioma
sections.content: A rare hamartoma of lymph vessels presenting in childhood. Size increases with head-down posture or Valsalva. Superficial: transilluminable cystic spaces (lid/conjunctiva) ± blood. Deep: gradual proptosis or acute pain/dVA due to haemorrhage (‘chocolate cyst’). CT shows low-density cyst-like mass and orbital enlargement. Treatment: Observation, sclerosing agents, bleomycin, Onyx® (ethylene-vinyl-alcohol co-polymer), surgery, or drainage of sight-threatening bleeds. Surgery is difficult (large/friable).

sections.title: Lymphoproliferative Diseases
content: Range: Benign hyperplasia to malignant lymphoma (85% B-lymphocytes). Classified by WHO system.
Benign Reactive Lymphoid Hyperplasia: Polyclonal, superolateral orbit (lacrimal gland). Gradual proptosis, ptosis, firm mass. Tx: Steroids, radiotherapy, rituximab. 25% progress to lymphoma in 5y.
Atypical Lymphoid Hyperplasia: Intermediate. Homogeneous pattern with larger nuclei.

Malignant Orbital Lymphoma: Low-grade B-cell (Non-Hodgkin’s). Commonest: Marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of MALT (40–70%). Bilateral in 25%. Systemic involvement in 40% (diagnosis) to 60% (5y). Tx: Radiotherapy, chemo, monoclonal antibodies.

sections.title: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis
content: Rare childhood proliferative disorder.
Spectrum: Benign unifocal 'Eosinophilic Granuloma' to disseminated 'Letterer–Siwe'.
Eosinophilic Granuloma: Orbital involvement common; rapid proptosis with superotemporal swelling.
Letterer-Siwe: May cause bilateral proptosis.
Treatment: Surgical excision is usually curative.

sections.title: Rhabdomyosarcoma: Pediatric Emergency
content: Commonest 1° orbital malignancy in children; 87% present before 15y (♂ bias 1.6:1).
Histology: Embryonal (commonest), Alveolar, Pleomorphic. Pluripotent mesenchymal origin.
Location: Intraconal (50%) or superior orbit (25%).
Clinical: Acute/subacute proptosis, ptosis, inflammation (mimics orbital cellulitis).
Imaging: US (irregular, well-defined, low/med reflectivity, high Doppler flow); CT/MRI (irregular mass ± bony erosion).
Management: Biopsy + Systemic work-up mandatory. Surgery for localized; Combined Radio+Chemo for extensive.

rows: Commonest adult mesenchymal orbital tumour. Middle-aged or children post-radiotherapy. Benign or malignant. Located superonasally. Gradual proptosis, pain, dVA, restricted motility. Tx: Complete excision. Recurrence common.
Uncommon. In 50% cases, precede diagnosis of primary tumour. Aggressive: rapid proptosis, restricted motility, CN involvement, inflammation.
Breast, Lung, Prostate, GI. Scirrhous (Breast/Gastric) may cause enophthalmos.

sections.title: Vascular Lesions: Orbital Varices
content: Definition: Uncommon congenital venous enlargements (medial orbit, usually unilateral).
Clinical: Intermittent proptosis/visible varix (worsens with Valsalva/coughing/head-down). Possible thrombosis/haemorrhage.
Investigations: CT/MRI show multiple masses, orbital wall expansion, and phleboliths.
Treatment: Surgery (difficult) if painful/disfiguring/sight-threatening. Radiological endovascular sclerosant/coil possible.

rows: High-flow: Direct ICA to Cavernous Sinus.
Low-flow: Dural arteries to Cavernous Sinus.
dVA, diplopia, audible bruit, pulsatile proptosis, orbital oedema, chemosis, iIOP, ophthalmoparesis (III/VI), vein engorgement, RAPD, disc swelling, ischemia.
Often asymptomatic; pain, cosmesis, chemosis, episcleral engorgement/arterialization, iIOP.
B-scan/Doppler US, CT, MRI: Dilated superior ophthalmic vein + thickened EOMs.
Embolization (success >85%). Visual loss occurs in 50% without Tx.
40% thrombose spontaneously. Tx reserved for glaucoma, dVA, diplopia, or severe pain.
